steps.title: Administrator dashboard
steps.body: The Lamassu dashboard is the administrator's side: you review how the DMS is configured and, at the end, the device and the certificate that result from the enrollment.

steps.title: Collapsed sidebar
steps.body: Collapsing the navigation sidebar leaves more width for the page and for the terminal. Each entry stays available as an icon.
steps.note: It only changes the layout of the dashboard; no configuration is modified.

steps.title: Device terminal
steps.body: The terminal plays the device, the EST client. It is a real shell in a disposable container with Bash, OpenSSL and curl, shown through an SSH web terminal; nothing in it is simulated.
steps.note: The account and password of that container are public and only valid for this throwaway demo environment.

steps.title: Registration Authorities
steps.body: A Registration Authority is the DMS: it defines the enrollment protocol, how devices are admitted and which CA signs their certificates.

steps.title: The EST Showcase DMS
steps.body: The page shows the ID est-showcase, the protocol EST · RFC 7030, the registration mode JITP, the authentication mode and the enrollment CA, Acme Device CA.
steps.note: The ID, not the display name, is the part that appears in the EST URL.

steps.title: Registration mode
steps.body: Just-in-time provisioning creates an unknown device automatically the first time it enrolls. Pre-registration would only admit devices registered beforehand.
steps.note: Allow replaceable enrollment is off, so enrolling again with an existing device ID is rejected: the demo uses a new ID.

steps.title: Enrollment CA and profile
steps.body: Acme Device CA, the Enrollment CA, signs every certificate issued through this DMS. The Device Certificates profile sets 365 days of validity, Digital Signature and Key Encipherment as key usage, and Client Auth and Server Auth as extended key usage.
steps.note: The profile enforces the extensions; the subject is copied from the CSR.

steps.title: Initial authentication
steps.body: With neither Require client certificate nor Call external webhook enabled, any device can request a certificate: the CSR is enough. That is what allows this demo to run over plain HTTP.
steps.note: A real DMS should require a client certificate (bootstrap) or a webhook. The Enroll and connect your first device quickstart uses CLIENT_CERTIFICATE over HTTPS.

steps.title: Private directory
steps.body: umask 077 makes every new file readable only by its owner, so the private key created next is not exposed. mkdir creates a directory named after the device and cd enters it.

steps.title: EST endpoint
steps.body: The terminal is a container, so it reaches Lamassu through host.docker.internal:8080, the host where the gateway runs. The EST path ends with the DMS ID, est-showcase, followed by the operation name.
steps.note: This demo uses HTTP on a local disposable environment; use HTTPS and verify the server certificate in any real deployment.

steps.title: Check cacerts
steps.body: The cacerts operation returns a Base64 PKCS#7 with the CAs the DMS distributes. Decoding it lists Acme Device CA and a second certificate of the gateway, because CA distribution includes the system CA.
steps.note: A successful answer shows the endpoint is alive; it does not prove that issuance works, and the bundle must not be trusted blindly.

steps.title: Device key pair
steps.body: openssl genpkey creates an EC P-256 key pair and writes it to device.key. The private key is never sent to Lamassu: only the CSR derived from it travels.
steps.note: Server-side key generation is disabled in this DMS, so the device must create its own key.

steps.title: Create the CSR
steps.body: The CSR carries the public key and the subject CN=sensor-0421, signed with the private key. With JITP, that CN becomes the device ID.
steps.note: The profile copies the subject from the request, so check the CN before sending it.

steps.title: Verify the CSR
steps.body: openssl req -verify checks that the self-signature matches the public key (it prints verify OK) and -subject shows the requested subject. The DMS repeats this check because Verify CSR signature is enabled.

steps.title: Encode for EST
steps.body: EST expects the request body as Base64-encoded DER PKCS#10. openssl converts the PEM CSR to DER and base64 -A writes it on a single line into device.csr.b64.

steps.title: Request the certificate
steps.body: A POST to simpleenroll with Content-Type application/pkcs10 sends the CSR. --fail-with-body makes curl fail on HTTP errors while saving the body, and the answer is written to enroll.b64. No client certificate is sent because initial authentication is disabled.
steps.note: After a timeout, do not repeat the request blindly: the certificate may already be issued, so check the device inventory first.

steps.title: Extract the certificate
steps.body: The response is a Base64 DER PKCS#7 that contains the certificate. openssl base64 -d decodes it and openssl pkcs7 -print_certs writes the PEM certificate to device.crt.
steps.note: Only the public certificate is written; device.key is not touched.

steps.title: Expand the terminal
steps.body: Expand makes the terminal pane use the full width without reloading either application, so long certificate lines stay on one line. Restore brings back the joint view.
steps.note: Both sessions stay alive; only the layout changes.

steps.title: Inspect the certificate
steps.body: openssl x509 prints the subject, the issuer, the serial number, the validity dates and the Key Usage and Extended Key Usage extensions. They must match the Device Certificates profile seen in the dashboard.
steps.note: -noout avoids printing the PEM, and the private key is never involved.

steps.title: Result of the enrollment
steps.body: The certificate has subject CN=sensor-0421, issuer Acme Device CA, Digital Signature and Key Encipherment, Client and Server Authentication, and a one-year validity. The serial is the value to compare in the dashboard.
steps.note: The terminal prints the serial in uppercase hexadecimal without separators; the dashboard shows it in lowercase pairs separated by colons.

steps.title: Restore the joint view
steps.body: Restore returns the dashboard and the terminal side by side, so the serial printed by the terminal stays visible while you check the dashboard.

steps.title: Devices inventory
steps.body: Devices lists every device Lamassu manages. The one that just enrolled appears here without anyone having created it in the console.

steps.title: Filter by device ID
steps.body: The device ID is the CN of the CSR, sensor-0421. Typing it in the filter narrows the inventory to that device.

steps.title: Open the device
steps.body: The record was created automatically when the DMS accepted the CSR; its Device ID is the CN you put in it. The page shows its status, its Registration Authority and its identity.

steps.title: Owner and identity
steps.body: The device belongs to the EST Showcase registration authority and its identity is ACTIVE at version v0, the first certificate issued to it. The page also shows when that identity expires.

steps.title: Associated certificate
steps.body: View certificate opens the certificate currently bound to the device identity, with its issuer, validity period and chain.

steps.title: Compare the serial
steps.body: The serial in the dashboard is the one openssl printed in the terminal, and the subject and issuer match too: the certificate the device obtained is the one Lamassu associated with it.
steps.note: This proves the association in Lamassu. It does not prove that the device installed or uses the key; the key never left the terminal.
